analysis.one_liner: Gives student loan borrowers new billing, servicing, and credit-reporting protections and bans forced arbitration on their loans.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced on December 5, 2023 with 8 Democratic cosponsors and referred to the Senate HELP Committee, which never held a hearing, markup, or vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would write a set of enforceable rights into law for people repaying student loans, both federal and private. It requires clear monthly statements, caps late fees, gives borrowers the right to have their payments applied in the way that saves them the most money, removes defaults from credit reports once a loan is repaid or consolidated, and requires loan companies to reach out to struggling borrowers with real repayment options instead of steering them into forbearance. It also brings federal loan servicing contractors under federal consumer financial law, lets state attorneys general enforce the rules, and bans mandatory arbitration and class-action waivers in student loan contracts.
analysis.who_benefits: The roughly tens of millions of Americans repaying federal or private student loans, especially borrowers in trouble: people behind on payments, borrowers whose loans were sold or transferred, servicemembers, and private loan borrowers whose contracts currently allow acceleration, co-borrower lock-in, and no discharge on death or disability.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Student loan borrowers in repayment or trouble

how_it_helps.text: Caps late fees at no more than 4 percent of the past-due amount, bars fees during a 15-day grace period, and bars charging more than one late fee per missed payment or per-loan fees for borrowers with multiple loans.
Requires loans to be prepaid without penalty and directs that extra payments be applied to the loan with the highest interest rate first, unless the borrower chooses otherwise.
Requires removal of the default record from a borrower's credit history once a defaulted loan is fully repaid or discharged through consolidation.
Creates a rehabilitation path for defaulted private loans: nine on-time payments over ten months removes the charge-off and related delinquency from the borrower's credit history.

Requires lenders and servicers to contact borrowers who are 30 or 60 days delinquent or who report hardship, tell them in plain terms about income-driven repayment, forgiveness, and discharge programs, and give them time to apply before the loan goes into default.

Makes federal student loan servicing contractors 'covered persons' under the Consumer Financial Protection Act, so the CFPB oversees them and state attorneys general can sue to enforce the law; it also bars contractors from using borrower data to market other financial products.
Bans mandatory pre-dispute arbitration clauses and class-action waivers in student loan contracts, allowing borrowers to sue in court.

Requires each private education loan to be cancelled on the borrower's death or total disability and sets rules for releasing co-borrowers, and bars lenders from denying credit to someone because they qualify for Servicemembers Civil Relief Act protections.
Requires prominent disclosures when a borrower refinances, listing which loans are federal and which federal benefits — income-driven repayment, forgiveness, deferment — would be given up.
Designates a servicemember and veterans liaison at every lender and servicer and bars reporting delinquency or default for borrowers on active duty in a combat zone.

analysis.who_pays: Student loan servicers and private student lenders bear the cost: staffing repayment-specialist offices and evening/weekend phone lines, building new billing and payment-allocation systems, losing late-fee and collections revenue, losing the ability to force borrowers into arbitration, and facing CFPB oversight and civil liability they did not previously have for federal loans.
analysis.who_pays_short: Loan servicers and private student lenders

drawbacks.text: The servicing mandates are detailed and expensive — trained repayment specialists, toll-free lines with limited wait times, availability after 5 p.m. and some weekends, itemized monthly statements — and servicers could pass those costs on to borrowers through other fees or the industry could consolidate further.

Mandatory discharge of private loans on death or total disability, forbearance on request for specified hardship categories, and a ban on acceleration clauses raise lenders' risk, which private lenders would likely offset with higher rates or tighter credit standards for new loans.

Some protections are not immediate: the CFPB must run a rulemaking process, and the bill allows delaying the effective date for federal servicing contractors by up to one additional year while the Education Secretary publishes recommendations.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The protections address documented pain points for borrowers — fee stacking, misapplied payments, defaults that linger on credit reports, and servicers steering struggling borrowers into forbearance — and the arbitration ban restores access to court. The compliance costs are real but are the ordinary cost of consumer financial regulation, and the bill allows a phased-in effective date. The bigger weakness is design-by-verbosity: the obligations are extremely granular, which invites compliance fights. On the whole, a borrower-friendly bill whose costs fall on the loan industry rather than on taxpayers or borrowers.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate HELP Committee on December 5, 2023, and sat there with no hearing, no markup, and no floor vote for the remaining thirteen months of the Congress.

narrative.text: Senator Dick Durbin introduced the bill on December 5, 2023 with fellow Democrats Klobuchar, Reed, Smith, Welch, Duckworth, and Warren as original cosponsors; the cosponsor list reached 8 Senate Democrats.
The same day it was introduced, the Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions.
No further action — no hearing, no committee vote, no floor action — is recorded for the rest of the 118th Congress, which ended January 3, 2025.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Student loan servicers, private student lenders, and collection agencies were spared the new CFPB oversight, liability, arbitration ban, and mandatory discharges the bill would have imposed. Borrowers gained nothing: defaults stayed on credit reports and servicing practices were unchanged by federal law.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Student loan servicers and private lenders

for.what_they_did: Introduced the Student Loan Borrower Bill of Rights and led it in the Senate.

against.name: Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on December 5, 2023 and took no recorded further action — no hearing, markup, or committee vote.

against.name: Sen. Bernie Sanders
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a markup or committee vote on the bill during the 118th Congress.

sides.party_line_note: All sponsors and cosponsors were Senate Democrats (8 total); no Republican signed on, and the Democratic-led committee never brought the bill to a vote.

industries.note: Federal servicing contractors would become 'covered persons' under the CFPB, barred from marketing other products with borrower data, required to staff repayment-specialist units and evening phone lines, and jointly liable for subcontractors. Their late-fee, forbearance-steering, and collections revenue would shrink, which is why this is a cost to them and a gain for borrowers.

Mandatory death and disability discharge, co-borrower release terms, a ban on acceleration clauses, forbearance on request, a rehabilitation program, and an arbitration ban all remove contractual advantages private lenders currently hold over borrowers.

The bill requires live outreach and repayment options before default, bars reporting active-duty combat-zone borrowers as delinquent, and protects borrowers from collection during inquiry disputes — shrinking the flow of loans pushed into collections.

Credit bureaus would be required to delete default records upon repayment or consolidation and charge-offs upon private loan rehabilitation, removing negative data that currently feeds their scoring products.
